scenarioIntro.S1: You are building an agent that resolves customer issues such as orders, refunds and account changes with backend tools, and escalates to people when needed.
scenarioIntro.S2: Your team uses Claude Code to write, refactor and document code, and wants consistent, shared configuration across the repository.
scenarioIntro.S3: A coordinator agent delegates searching, analysis and synthesis to specialised sub-agents and produces a cited report.
scenarioIntro.S4: You are building tools that help engineers explore unfamiliar codebases and automate routine work, using built-in tools and MCP servers.
scenarioIntro.S5: Claude Code runs in a CI/CD pipeline to review changes, generate tests and report findings without human interaction.
scenarioIntro.S6: A pipeline extracts structured fields from unstructured documents, validates them and routes uncertain results to people.

questions.stem: A retailer's support agent occasionally calls process_refund before verify_customer. Policy says identity must be verified first. What is the MOST reliable fix?
options: Gate process_refund in code so it returns a precondition error until verification succeeds
Switch to a larger model
Add 'ALWAYS verify the customer first' to the system prompt in capital letters so the rule stands out
Add a few-shot example to the prompt showing verification happening before every refund
notes: Ordering that matters must be enforced in code, not prose.
Doesn't address the missing enforcement.
Improves the odds; guarantees nothing.
Guides behaviour; doesn't enforce it.

questions.stem: A refund request is for 3,500 and the agent's limit is 2,000. Where should the limit be enforced?
options: In CLAUDE.md, alongside the other refund policies the agent should follow
In a PreToolUse hook that denies over-limit calls and returns guidance to escalate
In the process_refund tool description, stating the 2,000 limit and asking Claude to escalate above it
In a PostToolUse hook that reverses over-limit refunds
notes: Advisory.
PreToolUse blocks before execution.
Advisory.
Acts after money has moved.

questions.stem: Some support sessions end with a friendly closing message but no refund, no resolution record and no escalation. Best safeguard?
options: Raise the maximum iteration count so the agent always has enough turns to finish
Instruct the model in the system prompt never to end a conversation without resolving it
After the loop ends for any reason, check for a resolution or escalation record and escalate if neither exists
Increase max_tokens so the agent has room to complete the resolution step before ending
notes: More time isn't a guaranteed outcome.
Not a guarantee.
An orchestration-layer guarantee covers every exit path.
Unrelated to the outcome.

questions.stem: A coordinator delegates "find 2025–26 market data" to a search subagent, which returns irrelevant results because it didn't know the target market. Root cause?
options: The search tool's description is too long, so the subagent misread the query
tool_choice was set to auto, so the subagent chose its own search scope
The subagent's model is too small to infer the target market from the short task title
Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's context; the brief didn't include the market
notes: Not the cause.
Unrelated to context.
It still couldn't see missing context.
Context must be passed explicitly.

questions.stem: Final research reports regularly miss whole subtopics. Best fix?
options: Have the coordinator check coverage against the question and spawn follow-up subtasks for gaps
Have each subagent return longer, more exhaustive outputs so less is missed
Replace the multi-agent design with a single agent that researches everything
Lower the temperature
notes: The problem is overly narrow decomposition.
Doesn't add unassigned subtopics.
Loses the benefits of delegation without fixing coverage.
Unrelated.

questions.stem: An agent loop must decide whether to keep executing tools or return a final answer. Which signal should the code use?
options: Whether the reply text contains a completion phrase such as 'Task complete'
The response's stop_reason: continue on tool_use, finish on end_turn
A fixed number of iterations chosen per task type
Whether the response contains any text block at all
notes: Parsing prose is brittle: wording varies and can appear mid-task.
stop_reason is the structured, reliable signal. tool_use means Claude is waiting for tool results; end_turn means it has finished.
An iteration cap is a safety limit, not a completion signal.
Responses can contain text and tool_use blocks together; text doesn't mean the task is done.

questions.stem: A support agent's response has stop_reason "tool_use" with two tool_use blocks. What must the application send in the next request?
options: Nothing: the API executes client tools automatically and continues
A new user message summarising both tool results in plain text, without resending the assistant turn
The assistant turn as returned, then a user turn containing a tool_result for each tool_use_id
Only the result of the first tool, since Claude processes one tool at a time
notes: Client tools are executed by your code, not by the API.
Dropping the assistant turn breaks the tool_use / tool_result pairing.
Every tool_use block needs a matching tool_result (same tool_use_id), sent in a user message after the assistant turn.
Claude can request several tools in one turn; all of them need results.

questions.stem: A response comes back with stop_reason "max_tokens" in the middle of a long answer. What is the best handling?
options: Retry the identical request until a different stop_reason appears
Treat it like end_turn and show the answer to the user
Switch to the Message Batches API, which has no output limit
Treat it as truncated: raise max_tokens or continue, never present it as final
notes: The same limit will usually produce the same truncation.
The answer is cut off, so showing it as final is a correctness bug.
Batch requests use the same per-request max_tokens behaviour.
max_tokens means the output hit your cap, so the answer may be incomplete.

questions.stem: A tool call fails with a database timeout. The developer currently skips sending anything back and just calls the model again. What should happen instead?
options: Send a tool_result for that tool_use_id with is_error true and a structured description
Remove the tool_use block from the assistant turn and resend
Send an empty tool_result so the conversation history stays valid and the loop continues
End the session immediately with an error page
notes: Claude needs to know the call failed and why, so it can retry, choose another path or escalate.
Rewriting history hides the failure and can confuse later turns.
An empty result looks like success with no data, which leads to confident wrong answers.
Many failures are recoverable; the agent should get the chance to retry or escalate.

questions.stem: Why should every agent loop have a maximum-iteration limit, and what should happen when it is reached?
options: It isn't needed if stop_reason is checked correctly
To stop runaway loops; reaching it should trigger a handled outcome such as escalation
To make sure the agent finishes within one API call
To save tokens; when it's reached, the last response is returned to the user as the answer
notes: Agents can still loop, for example by retrying a failing tool repeatedly.
The cap is a safety net. Hitting it is an event to handle, not a silent exit.
Agents legitimately need many calls; the cap bounds them, it doesn't force one.
The last response may be mid-task, so returning it silently hides the failure.

questions.stem: Claude returns stop_reason "refusal" in an automated pipeline. What is the most appropriate design response?
options: Increase max_tokens so the model can finish
Treat it like end_turn and store the returned text as that item's final result
Handle it as its own outcome: log it and route the item for human review
Retry the same input a few times, since refusals are often transient
notes: Refusal is unrelated to the token limit.
Storing a refusal as a normal result corrupts downstream data.
A refusal is a deliberate safety stop; it needs its own handling path.
Repeated retries of a refused request are not an appropriate fix.

questions.stem: A chat assistant answers the first question correctly but on the second turn has no idea what the user said earlier. The server stores each user message in a database. What is the most likely bug?
options: The system prompt should tell Claude to remember previous turns
The model's context window is too small to hold two turns plus the system prompt
Prompt caching is disabled
The second request doesn't include the earlier messages in the messages array
notes: No instruction can make the model see messages that weren't sent.
Two short turns are far below any context limit.
Caching affects cost and latency, not what the model can see.
The Messages API is stateless: each request must contain the conversation history the model should consider.

questions.stem: Where does conversation state live in an application built on the Claude Messages API?
options: In the application, which resends the relevant history with every request
In the model's weights, updated after each turn
On Anthropic's servers, where each conversation is stored and keyed by API key
In the prompt cache, which keeps earlier turns available between requests
notes: The API keeps no conversation state between calls; your application owns it.
Models are not updated by individual conversations.
The Messages API doesn't store conversations between requests.
The cache only reuses identical prefixes you send; it isn't memory.

questions.stem: A long-running support conversation is approaching the context limit. Which approach keeps the agent accurate on key facts?
options: Rely on progressive summaries only, regenerated every few turns
Keep a compact case-facts block (IDs, amounts, decisions) in every request and trim older turns
Drop the oldest half of the messages so the most recent context is preserved
Ask the user to start a new chat and repeat their problem
notes: Repeated summarising gradually drops exact values such as amounts and IDs.
Critical facts are preserved verbatim while bulky history is reduced.
Blind truncation loses identifiers and decisions the agent still needs.
That's a poor experience and loses the verified state.

questions.stem: A search subagent keeps re-running searches the coordinator already completed, wasting time and tokens. What is the best fix?
options: Put a cache in front of the search API so repeated queries are cheaper
Use a smaller, faster model for the subagent to reduce the cost of repeats
Include the coordinator's findings and already-searched sources in the delegation brief
Give the subagent read access to the coordinator's full conversation
notes: Saves cost but doesn't stop redundant reasoning steps.
Doesn't address missing context.
Subagents start with isolated context; they only know what the brief tells them.
Floods its context and breaks isolation.

questions.stem: What is the main architectural benefit of delegating broad exploration to subagents in a multi-agent research system?
options: Subagents remove the need for a coordinator to synthesise results
Subagents are always cheaper because they automatically switch to smaller models
Subagents share one context window, so information is never duplicated
Each subagent uses its own context for exploration and returns a condensed result
notes: The coordinator still owns synthesis and conflict handling.
Model choice is configurable, not automatic.
Subagents have separate contexts; that's the point.
Context isolation is the key benefit; the coordinator receives summaries instead of raw dumps.

questions.stem: Which delegation brief is most likely to produce a useful subagent result?
options: Objective, known facts, scope limits, required output structure, and what to do if blocked
Only the output format, since the subagent can search for the rest
The coordinator's full conversation history, so the subagent has every detail it could possibly need
A one-line task title, so the subagent can interpret the work freely and creatively
notes: A complete, structured brief compensates for the subagent's isolated context.
Without the objective and known facts it repeats work or drifts.
Dumping everything floods the subagent's context and dilutes the task.
Too little context leads to generic or off-target results.

questions.stem: Subagents in a research system return long raw web pages to the coordinator, and the coordinator's quality drops on later steps. Best fix?
options: Give the coordinator a larger context window to hold the pages
Have subagents return condensed, structured findings with sources
Have the coordinator re-read every page itself to check the summaries
Run all subagents sequentially instead of in parallel
notes: More room delays the problem but keeps irrelevant content in context.
Accumulating raw tool output degrades the coordinator's context. Summaries with provenance keep it focused.
That defeats the purpose of delegation.
Ordering doesn't change how much raw content arrives.

questions.stem: A team builds a single agent with 22 tools covering search, code changes, tickets and deployments. Tool selection errors are frequent. Which redesign is most effective?
options: Set tool_choice to any so that at least one tool is always called on each turn
Add a paragraph to the system prompt listing when to use each tool
Split the work across specialised subagents, each with the few tools it needs
Rename the tools with numeric prefixes so they sort clearly
notes: Forcing a call doesn't help choose the right one.
Helpful but weaker than reducing the choice set.
Fewer, more relevant tools per agent improve selection accuracy and apply least privilege.
Names alone don't fix overlapping responsibilities.

questions.stem: Two subagents return conflicting figures for the same metric. What should the coordinator do?
options: Drop the metric so the report has no inconsistencies
Average the two figures and note that the value is an estimate
Pick the figure from the subagent that finished last, as it's the most recent
Keep both with sources and dates, and flag the conflict in the synthesis
notes: Hiding information isn't a fix; it removes value.
Averaging can produce a number no source supports.
Order of completion says nothing about accuracy.
Annotating conflicts preserves provenance and lets readers judge.

questions.stem: The main agent never delegates to a well-designed "security-reviewer" subagent defined with the Agent SDK. Which two things should you check first?
options: That the parent may use the subagent tool, and the subagent's description says when to use it
That max_tokens is above 8,000 and caching is enabled
That the subagent uses the same model as the parent, and that hooks are disabled
That the subagent has every tool the parent has, so it can complete any task
notes: Delegation needs the subagent tool to be permitted, and the description drives when the parent chooses it.
Neither setting controls delegation.
Model choice and hooks don't prevent delegation.
Subagents should get fewer tools; this isn't why delegation fails.

questions.stem: Invoices must always be extracted, validated, then summarised, in that order, with no variation. Which design fits best?
options: One prompt asking Claude to do all three steps in whatever order it judges best
A fixed pipeline (prompt chain) with each step as a defined stage
Three independent subagents running in parallel
A coordinator that dynamically plans subtasks for each invoice
notes: Loses the ability to validate between steps.
Predictable work with known steps suits a fixed pipeline: simpler, cheaper and easier to test.
The steps depend on each other, so they can't run in parallel.
Dynamic planning adds cost and variability where none is needed.

questions.stem: An investigation agent starts with a plan of four checks. After the first check it discovers the fault is in a third-party dependency. What should a well-designed agent do?
options: Stop and report that the original plan has failed and needs replanning by a human
Restart the whole investigation with a new plan from scratch
Adapt: add subtasks for the dependency and drop checks that no longer matter
Finish the original four checks before considering the new finding
notes: The finding is progress, not failure.
Discards useful work already done.
Open-ended investigation needs dynamic decomposition that responds to findings.
Running a fixed plan regardless of findings wastes effort and misses the cause.

questions.stem: A coordinator splits "impact of remote work on productivity" into two subtopics only. Reports keep missing major angles. Where is the fix?
options: In the final report: add a scope disclaimer listing the angles that weren't covered
In the search tool: return more results per query so subagents see more angles
In the subagents: ask each one to research its subtopic more broadly than assigned
In the coordinator: check coverage against the question and add subtasks for gaps
notes: A disclaimer doesn't fix missing coverage.
More results on two subtopics don't add new angles.
Subagents can't know what the coordinator never assigned.
Overly narrow decomposition is a coordinator responsibility.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes when to choose dynamic decomposition over a fixed pipeline?
options: When the needed steps depend on what is discovered along the way
Whenever the cheapest model is being used for the work
Whenever the task involves more than three steps or several tools
Whenever the final output must follow a strict JSON schema
notes: Dynamic decomposition is for open-ended tasks whose path can't be known up front.
Model choice doesn't determine the decomposition style.
Many-step tasks can still be fully predictable.
Output format is independent of how work is decomposed.

questions.stem: A refactoring task across a large codebase has an unknown number of affected modules. Which approach is most efficient?
options: Ask Claude to change every file in a single pass to keep the change consistent
Explore first to find affected modules, then create per-module subtasks
Estimate the number of modules and create that many placeholder tasks
Assign one subtask per top-level folder regardless of content
notes: Unscoped changes across a large codebase are risky and flood context.
Discovery-driven decomposition fits unknown scope.
Guessed tasks don't match real dependencies.
Fixed splits ignore where the change actually applies.

questions.stem: Policy: identity must be verified before an account address can be changed. Logs show the agent occasionally changes addresses first. Most reliable fix?
options: Add a few-shot example that shows verification happening first
State the verification rule in the system prompt in capital letters
Block the change-address tool in code until verification has succeeded
Lower the temperature so the agent follows the expected order more often
notes: Examples influence behaviour; they don't enforce it.
Raises the odds but guarantees nothing.
Order that matters must be enforced deterministically.
Randomness isn't the cause; nothing enforces the rule.

questions.stem: When a gated tool is called too early, what should the gate return to the model?
options: A generic 'Error' string, keeping internal rules hidden from the model
A success result with no data, so the agent moves on without an error
Nothing; the session should stop so a human can investigate the order
A tool_result with is_error true, a precondition category and the tool to call first
notes: Doesn't tell the agent what to do next.
Fake success misleads the agent.
Stopping wastes a recoverable situation.
A structured, actionable error lets the agent self-correct.

questions.stem: Which approach gives the strongest guarantee that a refund tool can never be executed before identity verification, at any point in a conversation?
options: A code gate or PreToolUse hook that checks verification state on every refund call
Force verify_customer with tool_choice on the first turn
List verify_customer first in the tools array so it is always considered before the refund tool
Describe the dependency in the refund tool's description
notes: Only a check on every call covers all turns, retries and long conversations.
Forcing controls one turn; later out-of-order calls are still possible.
Tool order in the array doesn't enforce call order.
Descriptions guide; they don't enforce.

questions.stem: An agent should not even consider the refund tool until an order has been looked up. Which technique directly achieves that?
options: Use tool_choice none on the first turn so no refund can happen early
Progressive exposure: add the refund tool only after the lookup succeeds
Put a warning in the refund tool's description to use it only after lookup
Set disable_parallel_tool_use to true so tools are called one at a time
notes: That blocks all tools, including the lookup.
If the tool isn't offered, it can't be chosen.
The tool remains selectable.
That limits parallel calls, not which tools are available.

questions.stem: Requirement: every support session must end either resolved or escalated to a person. Where should this be guaranteed?
options: By raising the iteration cap so the agent always has time to finish
By forcing escalate_to_human with tool_choice on every turn
At the orchestration layer: after the loop ends, check for a resolution or escalation record
In the system prompt: 'Never end a conversation without resolving or escalating'
notes: More time doesn't guarantee an outcome.
That would escalate everything, including easy cases.
A check outside the model covers every exit path: normal end, cap, error, refusal or timeout.
Prompts can't guarantee behaviour on every exit path.

questions.stem: An exception is thrown in the middle of an agent session and the process exits. With a well-designed orchestration layer, what happens?
options: The model retries the session automatically from the start
The user is asked to repeat their request in a new session
Nothing; exceptions are outside the scope of agent design
The safeguard sees no resolution was recorded and creates an escalation with a summary
notes: The model doesn't run your process lifecycle.
That loses context and is a poor experience.
Unhandled failures are exactly where customers get lost.
The guarantee must cover crashes too, not only clean exits.

questions.stem: A Claude Code or Agent SDK agent tends to stop before running the required checks. Which hook can enforce "don't finish until checks pass"?
options: A Stop hook that blocks stopping until the condition is met
A PostToolUse hook on the Read tool that checks results before continuing
A permissions deny rule that applies to the Stop event
A SessionStart hook that sets up the required checks
notes: Stop hooks run when the agent tries to finish and can send it back to work.
Runs after reads; doesn't control finishing.
Permission rules govern tool use, not lifecycle events.
Runs at the beginning, not at the end.

questions.stem: An agent escalates a billing dispute to a human. Which handoff content is most useful?
options: The full raw transcript, so the human has every detail exactly as it happened
Verified identity, facts established, actions taken, authorisation limits, open questions and reason
The model's internal reasoning for each turn, so the human understands its decisions
A one-line summary such as 'Customer unhappy about billing' to keep it quick to read
notes: Forces the human to re-read everything to find the key facts.
A structured package lets the human continue without repeating work or re-verifying.
Not a substitute for structured facts and status.
Too little; the human must start over.

questions.stem: Why include authorisation state (e.g. "verified via OTP", "refund limit reached") in a handoff package?
options: So the model can re-verify the customer automatically
Because the escalation API requires an authorisation field on every call
So the receiver doesn't repeat checks or act beyond what's been approved
To make the handoff more complete, since longer packages are reviewed faster
notes: The point is to avoid unnecessary re-verification.
No API requires this; it's a design best practice.
Authorisation state prevents duplicate verification and unauthorised actions.
Length isn't the goal; actionable state is.

questions.stem: A research pipeline passes work from a gathering stage to a writing stage. What should the handoff contain?
options: Only the final conclusions, without sources, so the writer's context stays small and focused
Raw search results, so the writer can decide independently what matters most
A list of the URLs visited, so the writer can open the pages it needs
Structured findings with source, date and confidence per claim, plus known gaps
notes: Loses traceability.
Pushes filtering work and context load downstream.
URLs alone don't carry the findings.
Provenance and gaps travel with the findings so the writer can cite accurately.

questions.stem: Policy: the agent may apply discount codes up to 20%; anything higher needs a manager. The agent occasionally applies 30% codes. Which fix is deterministic?
options: A PreToolUse hook on apply_discount that denies values above 20%
A PostToolUse hook that emails a manager after the discount is applied
Lowering the temperature so the model is more conservative
A sentence in the system prompt stating the 20% limit
notes: The check runs before every call, regardless of what the model decides.
Notifies after the fact; doesn't prevent it.
Not an enforcement mechanism.
Advisory only.

questions.stem: Tool results from a CRM include full customer phone numbers that the agent never needs. Which mechanism removes them reliably before the model sees them?
options: A PreToolUse hook that blocks the CRM lookup tool entirely
A PostToolUse hook or code wrapper that redacts those fields from the result
Lowering max_tokens so less of the tool output is processed
A system prompt telling the model to ignore phone numbers
notes: Blocks the needed lookup entirely.
Post-processing tool output deterministically minimises the data that reaches the model.
Unrelated to what data enters context.
The data still enters context.

questions.stem: Which statement about prompts and hooks is accurate?
options: Hooks only run in interactive sessions, not in automation
Prompts become enforced when written in capital letters
Prompt instructions are probabilistic; hooks are deterministic code
Hooks are suggestions that the model weighs alongside the prompt instructions
notes: Hooks run in SDK and non-interactive runs too.
Emphasis doesn't make instructions deterministic.
That's why must/never rules belong in hooks.
Hooks are executed by the harness, not interpreted by the model.

questions.stem: In a Claude Code command hook on PreToolUse, which exit code blocks the tool call and sends the hook's stderr back to Claude?
options: Exit code 0
Exit code 1
Any non-zero exit code
Exit code 2
notes: Exit 0 means success.
Exit 1 is a non-blocking error; the tool call proceeds.
Only exit 2 blocks.
Exit 2 is the blocking signal; stderr is fed back as feedback.

questions.stem: An audit requirement says every file write by the agent must be logged with path and timestamp. Best mechanism?
options: A PostToolUse hook on write and edit tools that appends to an audit log
A rule file describing the logging format the agent should use
Ask the model to report each write in its final answer
A custom slash command /log-writes that engineers run at the end of each session
notes: Runs after every successful write, independent of the model.
Rules are advisory.
Self-reporting can be incomplete.
Requires someone to remember to run it.

questions.stem: A code-review session from yesterday is resumed. Since then, 4 of 60 files have changed. What is the best approach?
options: Resume the session and trust all previous findings, as most files are unchanged
Resume with a summary of prior findings and re-analyse only the 4 changed files
Start a brand-new session with no prior context
Re-review all 60 files to be safe, since dependencies may have shifted
notes: Findings for the changed files may now be wrong.
Targeted re-analysis plus context injection avoids repeated work and stale conclusions.
Loses valid findings for 56 unchanged files.
Wastes effort and context.

questions.stem: You want to try a risky alternative design from an existing session without disturbing the original line of work. Which option fits?
options: Clear the session and start over
Use /compact before trying the alternative
Fork the session
Resume the session and try the alternative in place
notes: Loses the shared starting context.
Compacting summarises; it doesn't branch.
Forking branches from the same starting point while leaving the original intact.
Mixes both lines of work in one history.

questions.stem: A session's history is very long and mostly about an approach that was abandoned. What is the best way to continue?
options: Fork the session so the abandoned approach stays in a separate branch
Resume the full session as is, so no earlier detail is lost
Resume and ask Claude to ignore earlier turns
Start fresh with a short summary of the current state and open items
notes: The fork still carries the noisy history.
Keeps the abandoned approach in context.
The tokens are still in context.
Stale, noisy context hurts quality; a clean summary carries what matters.

questions.stem: Which practice makes long-running agent work most resilient to crashes and context resets?
options: Periodically writing progress, decisions and next steps to a state file
Relying on the conversation history, which already records every step in order
Increasing the context window so the history is never truncated
Disabling /compact so no detail is summarised away
notes: External state survives crashes and compaction.
History is lost or compacted.
Doesn't survive a crash.
Context still fills; crashes still happen.

questions.stem: An Agent SDK agent ignores the team's CLAUDE.md and project skills. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model needs extended thinking enabled to follow project conventions
Filesystem settings weren't loaded: setting_sources must include the project
CLAUDE.md is only read by the Claude desktop and terminal apps, not by the SDK
Skills must be pasted into the system prompt before the SDK can use them
notes: Unrelated to loading settings.
The SDK loads project settings such as CLAUDE.md and skills only when configured to.
Claude Code and the SDK can load it.
Skills load from the filesystem when enabled.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between building with the Client SDK (Messages API) and the Agent SDK?
options: The Agent SDK can't use custom tools, only the built-in ones it ships with
The Client SDK can't call tools; tool use requires the Agent SDK
The Agent SDK runs the tool loop and provides built-in tools; with the Client SDK you write the loop
The Agent SDK is model-agnostic, while the Client SDK is Claude-specific
notes: It supports custom tools and MCP servers.
The Messages API supports tool use; you run the loop.
That's the core trade-off: control versus built-in agent capabilities.
It's built on Claude.

questions.stem: You need a read-only analysis agent that must never modify files. Which configuration is most appropriate?
options: Allow all tools but lower max_tokens so edits can't be completed
Use acceptEdits permission mode so every change is logged for review
Tell the agent in the system prompt that it must never edit or write files
Restrict allowed tools to read-only ones such as Read, Grep and Glob
notes: Doesn't prevent writes.
That auto-approves edits, the opposite of what's needed.
Advisory only.
Least-privilege tool access enforces read-only behaviour.

questions.stem: In an automated CI agent, a rule says the agent must never modify files under .github/workflows/. Which mechanism is most reliable?
options: A PreToolUse hook or permission deny rule covering edits to that path
A clear note in the CI prompt listing every protected path the agent must not touch
A code review of the agent's changes after each run
Running the job with fewer iterations to limit its reach
notes: Deterministic enforcement applies even in unattended runs.
Advisory only.
Detects the change too late.
Doesn't prevent the edit.

questions.stem: A support agent's loop sometimes stops before the customer's issue is resolved. Which TWO loop-control practices are sound? (Select TWO.)
options: Use a fixed count of three iterations as the normal exit
End the loop when the reply text contains the word "resolved"
Treat any assistant text block as the end of the task
Continue while stop_reason is tool_use and finish on end_turn
Append each tool result to the history before the next request
notes: An arbitrary cap is a safety net, not a completion signal.
Parsing natural language for completion is fragile.
Text can accompany a tool call; it does not mean the work is done.
stop_reason is the reliable signal for whether Claude is waiting on tools.
The model needs the results to decide its next step.

questions.stem: A coordinator delegates analysis to sub-agents in a research system. Which TWO statements about sub-agents are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A sub-agent does not inherit the coordinator's conversation history
Sub-agents share one memory, so findings need not be passed on
Several sub-agents can be started in parallel from one coordinator turn
A sub-agent automatically receives every tool the coordinator has
Sub-agents should exchange results directly, bypassing the coordinator
notes: Sub-agents start with an isolated context.
There is no shared memory; context must be passed explicitly.
Multiple delegation calls in a single response run concurrently.
Tool access is configured per sub-agent.
Routing through the coordinator keeps the flow observable and controlled.

questions.stem: Refunds must never be issued before the customer's identity is verified. Which TWO mechanisms provide deterministic enforcement? (Select TWO.)
options: A prerequisite gate that blocks the refund tool until verification succeeds
A hook that intercepts the refund call and denies it without a verified ID
A lower temperature so that the agent follows the usual sequence
A system prompt line stating that verification always comes first
Three few-shot examples showing verification before the refund
notes: Code-level gates cannot be skipped by the model.
Hooks run every time, outside the model's control.
Sampling settings are not enforcement.
Prompt instructions have a non-zero failure rate.
Examples raise the likelihood but do not guarantee the order.

questions.stem: The team's issue-tracker MCP server must be available to everyone who clones the repo, and it needs an API token. What is the right setup?
options: Project scope .mcp.json, with the token referenced as ${TRACKER_TOKEN}

questions.stem: A CI step converts Claude's review into GitHub annotations and needs file, line, severity and message for each finding. Which approach is most robust?
options: Ask for a Markdown table and parse it with regex
Define the findings as a JSON schema (structured outputs or forced tool) and validate
Ask Claude to post the annotations directly in free text
Use a higher temperature so the findings are more detailed
notes: Fragile.
Schema-constrained output plus validation gives parseable, checked findings.
No validation step.
Unrelated to structure.

questions.stem: An extraction schema produces invented values for fields that are missing from some documents. Which TWO schema changes reduce fabrication? (Select TWO.)
options: Mark every field as required so that nothing is skipped
Remove the schema and accept free-form text instead
Add a field in which the model rates its own honesty
Allow null for fields that may be absent from the source
Add enum values such as "unclear" or "other" with a detail field

Loses structure without reducing invention.
Self-assessment does not prevent fabricated values.

questions.stem: A team is considering the Message Batches API. Which TWO workloads suit it? (Select TWO.)
options: A weekly audit report that nobody is waiting on
Nightly generation of test suggestions for the next morning
A pre-merge check that blocks developers until it finishes
A multi-turn tool-calling loop inside a single batch request

questions.stem: Mid-conversation, a customer writes "Stop. I want to talk to a real person." The agent has a likely fix ready. What should happen?
options: Escalate immediately with a structured handoff package
Ask the customer to confirm they really want a human
Run sentiment analysis to decide
Apply the fix, then offer escalation if they're still unhappy

questions.stem: Two credible sources give different market sizes for the same year. What should the synthesis do?
options: Use the larger figure, since it's more likely to include all segments
Present both with source attribution and dates, noting the conflict
Average the two figures to give a balanced estimate
Drop the figure so the report contains no contradictions
notes: Arbitrary.
Preserve provenance and annotate conflicts.
Unsupported figure.

questions.stem: A research subagent's web search fails with a timeout. What should it return?
options: The message 'No relevant sources found', so the report stays readable
Results drawn from its own training knowledge, so there's no gap

questions.stem: Overall extraction accuracy is 97%, but finance reports frequent wrong bank details on scanned forms. Best review design?
options: Randomly review 5% of all documents, increasing to 10% during busy periods
Review every document whose overall extraction accuracy falls below 97%
Ask the model for an overall confidence score and review below 0.9

questions.stem: After several rounds of summarising a long support conversation, the agent quotes the wrong refund amount. What is the likely cause?
options: Progressive summarisation lost the exact figure; keep key facts in a case-facts block

The model struggles with exact numbers in long conversations
Prompt caching returned an earlier, outdated response

questions.stem: A critical instruction placed in the middle of a 120k-token prompt is often ignored. What is the best mitigation?
options: Lower the temperature so the model follows instructions more strictly
Put critical instructions at the start or end, or in a compact block near the question
Repeat the instruction in capital letters in the same position
Add more supporting documents so the instruction stands out

questions.stem: An agent's context fills with raw tool outputs (logs, full JSON, whole pages) after a few steps. Best practice?
options: Restart the agent after every tool call to clear its context
Disable any tool that can return large outputs
Trim tool results to what's needed and delegate bulky reads to subagents
Keep everything, since more context generally leads to better-informed answers
notes: Loses all continuity.

Tool-result accumulation is a major source of context degradation.
Irrelevant content dilutes attention.

questions.stem: What belongs in a case-facts block for a support agent?
options: Every tool result received so far, in full
The model's tone and style instructions for this customer
The full transcript, so nothing from the conversation is ever lost or paraphrased
Stable, verified facts: IDs, amounts, dates, verification status and decisions

questions.stem: During a long coding session, Claude uses /compact. Which practice prevents important details from being lost?
options: Keep key findings and decisions in a notes file that survives compaction
Compact after every message to keep the context small
Increase max_tokens before compacting so more is kept
Never use /compact, so no details are summarised away

questions.stem: A customer asks for a refund type that no policy covers. What should the agent do?
options: Approve it, since the customer is probably right
Escalate to a human; don't invent a policy
Apply the closest existing policy without saying so
Deny it, since it isn't listed

questions.stem: Which signal is the LEAST reliable trigger for escalation?
options: An action exceeding the agent's authorisation limits
No progress after several attempts at a fix
Detected negative sentiment in the customer's tone
An explicit request to speak to a person
notes: A clear policy trigger.
A reliable trigger.
Tone doesn't reliably indicate whether the agent can resolve the issue.

questions.stem: A routine password reset request comes in, and the agent has the tools to complete it. The customer sounds frustrated. What should the agent do?
options: Ask the customer to try again later when calmer
Escalate all account-related requests by default
Escalate, because a frustrated customer is better served by a human
Resolve it autonomously, efficiently and empathetically

questions.stem: An agent has tried three different approaches to fix a sync issue, and each failed. What now?
options: Escalate with a summary of what was tried and the results
Close the ticket and ask the customer to open a new one

Route it for approval or escalate, with the case details
Refuse the request without further explanation

Delay the report until every source is available again

Logging every error with enough context to debug it
Returning structured errors that state whether a retry makes sense
Escalating to a human after repeated failures

That page 3 fields couldn't be read, with a reason, so they're routed for review

questions.stem: Which combination best sustains coherent exploration of a very large codebase across sessions?

questions.stem: An extraction pipeline currently sends a random 5% sample of documents to human review. Errors in critical fields still reach finance. Best redesign?
